A 87-year-old man with a history of dementia is brought in by his daughter due to increased agitation.
She reports that his primary care physician conducted a thorough evaluation last week, including
laboratory and imaging studies, which were unremarkable. The patient struggles to describe any pain
or discomfort. During an osteopathic structural examination, the greater wings of the sphenoid are
palpated as superior relative to the occiput, which feels inferior in the vault hold. What additional

findings are most likely in this patient? Answer Choices: (A) Dysfunction of the tentorium cerebelli due
to cranial base strain (B) Torsional strain pattern with left sphenoid rotation (C) Superior deviation of
the occiput at the sphenobasilar synchondrosis (D) Caudad deviation of the sphenoid at the
sphenobasilar synchondrosis (E) Presence of a physiologic craniosacral strain pattern (F) Restricted
craniosacral rhythmic impulse (CRI) (G) Favoring of the extension phase in craniosacral motion (H)
Compression of the sphenobasilar synchondrosis (I) Exaggeration of the flexion phase in craniosacral
motion (J) Vagal nerve entrapment at the occipitoatlantal joint
 A. Compression of the sphenobasilar synchondrosis
B. Exaggeration of the flexion phase in craniosacral motion
C. Favoring of the extension phase in craniosacral motion
D. Vagal nerve entrapment at the occipitoatlantal joint
E. Restricted craniosacral rhythmic impulse (CRI)
F. Dysfunction of the tentorium cerebelli due to cranial base strain
G. Presence of a physiologic craniosacral strain pattern
H. Superior deviation of the occiput at the sphenobasilar synchondrosis
I. Caudad deviation of the sphenoid at the sphenobasilar synchondrosis
J. Torsional strain pattern with left sphenoid rotation
